title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All planned pairs completed (complete_pairs = 200) consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact two‑sided McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, deterministic execution accounting that enforces the shared‑initial semantics, the Mininet 10% randomized holdout (20 tasks) that produced zero validator–emulator disagreements, and a focused discussion of methodological tradeoffs, validator coverage, and concrete recommendations for follow‑up studies (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises NetOps productivity gains but risks producing incorrect or unsafe changes that cause outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore advocates grounding and verifier–assisted repair (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. However, the practical marginal benefit of automated repair depends on (1) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under the deployed generation policy, (2) validator coverage and fidelity, and (3) the available repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered and executed a narrowly scoped confirmatory question: Does an automated, deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? Our contributions are: (i) a sealed preregistered paired experiment (n = 200) that isolates the marginal effect of a validator+single‑repair step on the identical generated candidate per task; (ii) full execution accounting showing that every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator (n11 = 200), producing a precise null outcome; and (iii) artifact‑grounded methodological clarifications and operational recommendations about when GVR is likely to be beneficial.
sections.related_work: LLM applications across domains exhibit factual errors, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism; mitigations include retrieval grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, and guarded agent architectures. NetOps prototypes show feasibility of intent→configuration generation but typically lack instrumented, production‑like failure‑rate evaluations (e.g., NetConfEval and other intent‑driven configuration studies). Architectural proposals recommend combining LLMs with deterministic validators (Batfish‑style checkers) and guarded agents to reduce unsafe outputs, while red‑team audits document configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection vectors that can alter safety outcomes. Our study aims to supply an externally auditable, preregistered measurement that isolates the marginal effect of deterministic repair for a fixed model and sampling policy, complementing prior prototype and threat‑analysis work.
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration. The study (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) predeclared a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one deterministic shared initial generation per task, and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call when the primary validator reported violations. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; the primary test was an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Confidence intervals were computed via bootstrap percentile (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729).

Task bank and validators. The confirmatory sample comprised a machine‑checkable intent→configuration task bank (200 tasks, four topology clusters). Each task encodes initial and expected final state, workflow constraints (make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields, group‑active minima), and a required_sequence. The primary deterministic checker enforces syntactic and intent/constraint checks and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator served as a preregistered secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator blind spots at the data‑plane level.

Shared‑initial semantics and determinism. The adapter semantics used in the execution enforce a shared_initial generation: for each task a single generated candidate was produced and reused for both baseline and guarded conditions so the paired comparison isolates the marginal effect of validation and (if invoked) repair on the identical candidate. The preregistration also stated deterministic generation intent (temperature=0). In the archived execution artifacts the model configuration records a null temperature field, but adapter accounting and the deterministic reconciliation artifacts demonstrate that the adapter enforced the shared‑initial deterministic semantics at runtime (hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; stage_counts indicate a single shared_initial_generation per task). In other words, determinism was achieved by adapter‑enforced shared reuse of a single generation per task rather than by relying solely on the model configuration temperature field. This explicit enforcement and the provider‑call audit entries are the basis for our claim of deterministic paired comparisons; these execution records are archived in the bundle for auditability.

Contamination detection, exclusions, and reproducibility gap. The preregistered contamination plan used the Mininet emulator as an independent end‑to‑end check for a randomized 10% holdout. The contamination summary reports zero disagreements for that holdout (20 tasks). We disclose a reproducibility gap: the explicit labeled randomized selection seed used to draw the Mininet holdout is not present among the labeled artifacts, which prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of the holdout draw even though the contamination summary is recorded. Per the preregistration, any pair flagged for validator–emulator disagreement would have been excluded from the primary analysis; no such exclusion was necessary in this run.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. All planned episodes completed: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions), complete_pair_count = 200. Model calls used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); repair calls used = 0 because no validator failures occurred. Adapter/provider audit records confirm hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, and stage_counts consistent with one shared initial generation per task.

Primary outcomes and exact inference. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed paired difference estimate is 0.0. The prespecified exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile confidence intervals (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) produce a 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand and test the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis cannot be evaluated because baseline validator failures are absent.

Secondary outcomes and contamination check. Because no validator failures occurred, no repair prompts were emitted and the preregistered secondary estimands (repair iteration distributions, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) have no empirical data in this run. The Mininet 10% holdout contamination check reported zero validator–emulator disagreements across the 20 sampled tasks; interpretation of that zero disagreement result is conditional on the holdout selection (see Methods reproducibility gap). Representative validator diagnostics in the archived traces indicate tasks included nontrivial dependency patterns (difficulty labels such as "medium", "hard", and "very_hard" and patterns like make_before_break_uplink_switchover), yet the generator/prompt pair produced sequences that satisfied the machine‑checkable constraints for the sampled tasks.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The artifact‑grounded null outcome (zero validator failures) is not evidence that repair is universally unnecessary; it is a precise, reproducible statement that, for this curated task bank and the frozen shared‑initial generation policy, there were no validator‑detectable failures for GVR to reduce. The paired shared‑initial design intentionally isolates the marginal effect of validation+repair on a fixed generator output and therefore excludes gains obtainable by re‑sampling the LLM (e.g., producing alternative failing candidates that a repair could correct).

Methodological tradeoffs. The shared‑initial paired design increases internal control but restricts exploration of unconditional failure prevalence. To estimate unconditional operational failure risk or the unconditional marginal benefit of repair, future studies should include independent per‑condition multi‑sample draws and nonzero‑temperature sampling to surface diverse failure modes. Similarly, expanding the repair budget (multi‑step repairs or human‑in‑the‑loop escalation) and scaling emulation checks will allow empirical evaluation of repair effectiveness and of GVR‑introduced failure modes.

Validator coverage and operational implications. Deterministic validators codify a set of syntactic and policy checks but cannot capture all device idiosyncrasies. The Mininet holdout provided a pragmatic secondary check and produced no disagreements in the sampled 20 tasks, but the missing labeled selection seed limits exact reconstruction of that draw. Operational deployment should combine richer device models, larger emulation/testbed sampling, adversarial perturbation tests, and recorded selection seeds to probe validator blind spots and to quantify residual risk. When baseline validator failures are rare under the intended generation policy, resources may be better invested in expanding validator fidelity and adversarial testing rather than in a single‑pass automated repair budget.
sections.conclusion: We executed a sealed preregistered paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic validator. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent. The results emphasize that GVR’s marginal value is workload dependent: when validator‑detectable failures are already rare for the chosen generator/prompt policy, a single automated repair attempt yields no measured benefit for validator‑detected errors. Future confirmatory work should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, record selection seeds for emulator holdouts, evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model policies, and explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets to quantify practical operational gains.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraint: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Orchestration and experiment generation used hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Determinism enforcement: the adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics so a single generated candidate per task was reused across baseline and guarded conditions; adapter/provider accounting and the deterministic reconciliation artifacts record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts consistent with one shared_initial_generation per task, which is how deterministic paired comparisons were achieved at runtime despite a null temperature field recorded in the model configuration. Contamination check: a Mininet‑based emulator was preregistered and executed on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks); the contamination summary artifact reports zero disagreements for that holdout. Known reproducibility gap: the labeled artifacts do not include the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw the 10% Mininet holdout; this omission prevents bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of the holdout selection even though the contamination check result is archived. Execution accounting and artifacts: model calls used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; after the autonomy lock no human manually edited or selectively rewrote technical manuscript content. No post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
